log: When this completion became a `PendingEffect` handler it moved to module scope, lost `this`, and started writing to the terrain feature registry singletons instead of the ones the action was constructed with. Invisible in the game, which uses the singletons; wrong for anything with registries of its own.

`ClearForest.complete(action)` is the original closure body, verbatim with `this` read as `action`, and `registerDelayedAction` now hands the handler the action that was performed. Static rather than an instance method: a new public member makes the class unassignable to `Action` (`DataObject._keys: (keyof this)[]`), and a static method may still read its instances' private fields.
Requires core-unit ^0.1.23, which passes the performed action through.

46 rules now carry an id — `civ1-city:<dir>/<file>/<what it does>`, e.g. `civ1-city:city/created/register` — so a variant can `replace`, `disable`, or order a rule `before`/`after` another by reference instead of outbidding it with a priority number.

Named for what each rule does rather than numbered by position, because a position id breaks the moment a rule is inserted above it. Rules built in a loop take the loop's class names — `${TerrainType.name}` and so on — which survive the production bundle because esbuild runs with `keepNames`.

Raises core-rule to ^0.1.5: 0.1.4 reads a leading string as a priority, so these rules throw `priority(...).value is not a function` against it. The range said `^0.1.0`, which would have let a consumer with an older lockfile install exactly that.

`446c15a` was formatted with prettier 3, which adds trailing commas to parameter lists and call arguments. This package pins prettier 2, whose `prettier:format` removes them again — so the next forced rebuild, in a publish wave or anywhere else, rewrote these files as a side effect.
Formatting only, no behaviour change. Separated from the rule ids that follow so neither diff hides in the other.

`city.player()` was read at assertion time, after `city.capture(enemy)` had reassigned it, so all three assertions compared against the enemy. It passed for years anyway: with `#private` fields two `Player`s had no enumerable state, and deep equality could not tell them apart. Stage 1 made `_id` enumerable and the assertion started meaning something.
The player is captured before the city changes hands. Inverted once to confirm it fails when it should.

`buildCost(Item, cost, 'civ1-unit:city/build-cost')` names each rule `civ1-unit:city/build-cost/Warrior`, so a variant can replace a unit's cost rather than outbid a rule it cannot address. Costs are among the likeliest things a variant changes, and they are all built here, hidden from callers who never see the `new BuildCost(…)`. Without a prefix nothing changes.
Also raises core-rule to ^0.1.5, the first version that accepts an id.

`discharge(effect, ...context)` hands the handler whatever the discharger has in hand that the effect could not carry. A delayed action passes the action it performed, so completion can use the registries that action was constructed with instead of the singletons a handler registered at import reaches for.
A handler must not need it: an effect discharged after a load has only what the save held. Additive — handlers taking one argument are unaffected.

Format 1 was written with a top-level `pendingEffects` array — always empty — and `hydrate` refused a file with anything in it, because effects had no saveable shape until rules had identities. Stage 6 gave them the ordinary one: a `PendingEffect` is a `DataObject` in the `pendingEffects` registry slot, so it travels in `entities` and `registries` like everything else, and both Darwin's Voyage and the ten delayed actions round-trip that way.

So the field is gone from the type and from what `save` writes, and the refusal is gone from `hydrate`. Older files still carry `"pendingEffects": []`, which nothing reads, so the format number stays 1.

The package had a test script and no tests, so the publish gate could only report "not run" — every guarantee it makes was proved in web-renderer's suites instead, against a whole seeded game. These need nothing but a Game and a two-node entity:

encode writes entities as references, classes as names, registry fields as arrays, and round-trips maps and sets through decode; it refuses a nameless function by field path, and decode refuses a dangling reference.
save refuses without a plugin manifest, finds entities no registry lists by following references, and carries a pending effect as an ordinary entity.
hydrate restores a cycle without running a constructor, loads a format-1 file still carrying the old empty placeholder, and a re-save is byte-identical.
assertCompatible refuses an unreadable format and a missing plugin, and reports version drift instead of refusing.

Writing them found one real gap, recorded in the test rather than fixed here: `{ handler: () => {} }.handler` is not anonymous — the property key names it — so a named closure in a field is written as `{ $class: 'handler' }` and fails only on load. Closing that means checking every `$class` against the class registry at save time.
Also corrects the refusal message, which still pointed at Stage 6 for rule identity, and refreshes the lockfile, which predated three of the package's own dependencies.

The completions were closures bound to `this`, so they wrote to the registries the action was constructed with. Converting them to `PendingEffect` handlers moved them to module scope, and six of the ten swapped those registries for `…Instance` singletons. The game never noticed, because `defaultGame` is the singletons; every test with its own registries did. `civ1-unit`'s "should clear Fortified when activated" watched `Fortified` land in a registry it was not looking at.

`delayedBusy` holds the performed action, so it now passes it through `discharge`, and `registerDelayedAction` hands it to `complete` — as a third argument, not the first, so packages written against the two-argument form keep working. After a load there is no performed action, and the `action` factory rebuilds one with defaults, which is all a load can do until plugins register against a game rather than at import.
Requires core-pending-effect with discharge context.
